title: Descriptive Statistics in jamovi
section: Descriptive Statistics for the Entire Sample
text:
Descriptive Statistics for the Entire Sample
Using the Climate Change Trust Scale (Barchard, Hoffman, Okagawa, & Odents, 2021), we asked participants to tell us how much they trusted politicians and scientists, with response options 1 = None at all, 2 = A little, 3 = Moderate, 4 = A lot, 5 = A great deal. You will determine who participants trust more.

Under the Exploration menu, click Descriptives.



Calculate descriptive statistics for the variable CCTS_Politicians_Say (“How much do you trust what politicians say about climate change?”) and variable CCTS_Scientists_Say (“How much do you trust what scientists say about climate change?”).
Ask it to calculate three statistics that measure Central Tendency: Mean, Median, and Mode.
Ask it to calculate three statistics that measure Dispersion: Standard Deviation, Variance, and Range.


Check your answers

title: Descriptive Statistics in jamovi
text:
Descriptive Statistics for Subsamples
Often researchers are interested in particular groups of participants. Here, we will calculate trust separately for people who identify as female, male, and non-binary.

To create another analysis without erasing the old one, click Exploration, then Descriptives.
Calculate descriptive statistics for the same two variables: CCTS_Politicians_Say (“How much do you trust what politicians say about climate change?”) and variable CCTS_Scientists_Say (“How much do you trust what scientists say about climate change?”). However, this time, split the results by Gender.
Calculate the same six statistics as last time: mean, median, mode, standard deviation, variance, and range.

Who trusts politicians the most: people who identify as female, male, or non-binary?
MalesFemalesNon-binary people
Who trusts scientists the most: people who identify as female, male, or non-binary?
MalesFemalesNon-binary people

title: Introduction to jamovi
text:
The purpose of this exercise is to introduce you to jamovi, a powerful, easy-to-use statistics program that is also FREE. You can install jamovi on your Windows, Mac, Linux, or Chromebook. If you do not have access to one of those types of computers, you can use jamovi in a simple online format. In this exercise, you will learn the basics of jamovi and then use it to calculate some probabilities.
During this exercise, you will explore probabilities related to sustainability. If you want to learn more about sustainability and climate change, see What You Can do About Climate Change.

title: Introduction to jamovi
text:
Calculate Simple Probabilities
Calculate the percentage of participants who often wish or almost always wish they behaved more sustainably. To do this:

Click the Frequencies menu.
In the Contingency Tables section, click Independent Samples.
Move the variable PRCC17 (“I wish I behaved more sustainably.”) to Rows. To do this, highlight the variable PRCC17. Then click the arrow that points to the right to move this variable into the box that says Rows.
Move Gender to Columns.
Look at the right-hand side of jamovi, where it shows your output. You should see a Contingency Table with four columns and six rows.


Columns are vertical. You should have columns for Female, Male, Non-binary, and Total.
Rows are horizontal. You should have rows for Never, Rarely, Sometimes, Often, Almost always, and Total.
Cells are the intersections of rows and columns. There should be 24 cells in your table; each cell should have a number in it.


Look at the left-hand side of jamovi, again, where you tell it what analysis you want to do. In the Cells section, check the box to indicate you want the Percentages for Row.
In the output table, look at the row that says Total. Read off the percentage of participants who are male.


Note that jamovi considers percentages to be 2 decimals. For example, 32% is 2 decimals, whereas 32.78% would be 4 decimals. In this course, we will present results to 2 decimals.

Question 1: What percentage of participants are male (whole number)? 

In jamovi, in the Cells section, indicate you want the Percentages for Column. To make the output easier to read, uncheck the box that shows the Percentages for Row.
In the output table, look at the column that says Total.


22% of participants said they often wish they behaved more sustainably.
Find the percentage who said they almost always wish they behaved more sustainably.
Add these percentages together.

Question 2: What percentage of participants often or almost always wish they behaved more sustainably (whole number)?

title: Introduction to jamovi
text:
Calculate a Joint Probability
A joint probability is the probability of two events occurring simultaneously. Calculate the percentage of participants who are female and who rarely wish they behaved more sustainably. To do this:

In the Cells section, indicate you want the Percentages for Total. To make your output easier to read, you can uncheck the box for Column.
On your output table, look in the cell for female and rarely. Read off the percentage of participants who are female and rarely wish they behaved more sustainably.

Question 3: What percentage of female participants rarely wish they behaved more sustainably (whole number)?

title: Introduction to jamovi
text:
Calculate a Conditional Probability

A conditional probability is the probability of one event occurring assuming another event has already occurred. For those people who almost always wish they behaved more sustainably, calculate the percentage who are female. To do this:
In the Cells section, indicate you want percentages for Row.To make your output easier to read, you can uncheck the box for Total.
Look at the row of results for almost always. Of participants who almost always wish they behaved more sustainably, read the percentage who are female.

Question 4: What percentage participants who almost always wish they behaved more sustainably are female? (whole number)?

title: Introduction to jamovi
text:
How to Delete Output
If you made any mistakes when you were working, you might need to remove a portion of your output. For example, if you did the same analysis twice, you should delete the extra analysis. To delete a portion of your output:

Right click the title for that part of your output.
From the drop-down menu, click Analyses.
From the side-menu, click Remove.

title: Introduction to jamovi
text:
Save and Export

Now that you have answered all the questions, save them all in a Word file. This way, you’ll have all of your answers.
Save your jamovi file again, so that you have everything you did. This file will be helpful in the future.
Export your jamovi output to a pdf file. To do this,


Click the three horizontal bars on the top left of your jamovi screen.
Click Export.
Enter a file name that includes your full name, the assignment name, and the word Output. Example: “Rick Astley PSY422 Introduction to jamovi Output.pdf”
Select Portable Document Format (.pdf).
Click Export.

title: About
text:
These interactive tutorials will guide you through the basics of using jamovi, which is free statistical software. You will download and use real data and check your results as you go (you can retry as many times as you like).
The tutorials are based on the free assignment series, “Jamovi for Intro Stats - Climate Change Data”, by Kimberly A. Barchard, Joshua Galloway, Jaidyn Billerbeck and Fred Vincent Margallow, available on the OSF. The data used is real data which was collected by the authors using the online recruitment service Mechanical Turk in 2021.
